records.title: PERCEPTUAL FLUENCY AND PREFERENCE REVERSAL
records.abstract: We examined how perceptual fluency affects risk preference judgments and explored 1 important boundary condition for its effect. All participants were presented with a lottery scenario that required them to choose between a lottery ticket and a coupon that they could redeem when making a purchase or to set a price at which they would sell the same lottery ticket. Perceptual fluency was elicited by asking participants to read the scenario set out in a way that was either easy or difficult to understand. The results showed that when the likelihood of getting a desirable outcome was relatively high, participants who experienced decreased perceptual fluency tended to be risk aversive in the choice task but risk seeking in the pricing task. Accordingly, several mechanisms are discussed that potentially underlie this preference reversal effect along with theoretical and practical implications of our findings.

records.title: Persuading the proxy: a framework for AI-mediated marketing decisions
records.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
records.abstract:
This paper reconceptualizes persuasion in hospitality marketing in response to the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that curate, filter and increasingly autonomously book hospitality services. Traditional persuasion models assume a human cognitive target; however, AI agents now function as parallel decision-makers whose algorithmic evaluations shape customer choices. This study aims to articulate how persuasion operates when influence must target both human customers and AI agents.
 
 
 
 This conceptual study synthesizes research from hospitality marketing, AI-enabled customer decision-making and agentic systems. Drawing on interdisciplinary evidence, it develops the Dual-Target Persuasion Framework, which differentiates between AI-assisted and AI-autonomous pathways and integrates key mediators (i.e. trust, cognitive load, preference alignment and perceived agency) and moderators (i.e. service type, technological fluency and emotional salience).
 
 
 
 The framework proposes that persuasion in AI-mediated hospitality environments is bifurcated: one pathway targets human psychology through AI-assisted decision support, while the other targets algorithmic evaluation through machine-readable signals and structured data. The effectiveness of the influence depends on how mediating mechanisms operate across these two pathways and on boundary conditions that determine when human judgment or agentic optimization dominates. Customer loyalty, satisfaction and decision quality increasingly emerge from a hybrid interplay between human sentiment and agentic logic.
 
 
 
 This study offers guidance to hospitality managers designing content for two distinct persuasion targets. Effective strategies must combine emotionally resonant narratives for customers with structurally optimized, verifiable and machine-readable information for AI agents. The framework highlights how data quality, transparency and preference alignment influence an agent’s selection processes and how experiential framing and agency preservation support human acceptance of AI-mediated recommendations.
 
 
 
 This paper advances persuasion theory by identifying AI agents as legitimate persuasion targets and offering the first hospitality-specific account of dual-path influence in AI-mediated decisions. It reframes persuasion as a continuum from AI assistance to autonomy and outlines a forward-looking research agenda on customer–AI–brand interactions in environments where loyalty may be shaped as much by algorithmic selection as by human cognition.

records.title: Popular pleasures: Sharpening the tools for a popular aesthetic in video game criticism
records.abstract: What is the purpose of popular aesthetics in video game criticism? This overarching question will serve as a starting point in this article, which is an attempt to bring the focus of game studies back to popular aesthetics in general and the aesthetic category of ‘cuteness’ in particular. As popular media pose problems for established aesthetic theories, I want to explore the most classical of all aesthetic theories, Immanuel Kant’s Critique of the Power of Judgment, in order to point towards the possibility of a popular aesthetic. The aesthetic judgement of cuteness, more concretely Yoshi’s Crafted World’s cuteness, guides us through this reflection. Cuteness finds its place as ‘impure’ beauty, characterized by a specific constellation between the agreeable, useful and beautiful. By interrogating the strengths and weaknesses of Kant’s aesthetics, I identify three points to carve out a popular video game criticism in the future: (1) the role of the body for sensory cognition, (2) the question of aesthetic form and (3) the emphasis on popular pleasures.

records.title: Processing fluency and judgment
Reading fluency and word segmentation agreement modulate the benefits of word boundary cues for older readers in traditional Chinese
records.abstract: Despite having extensive reading experience, older readers suffer from declines in visual acuity and processing speed, which may undermine their ability to segment words in unspaced scripts like Chinese. While using text colors to highlight word boundaries can aid reading and eye movement control for readers of simplified Chinese, it remains unclear whether the benefits extend to older readers, especially those who read the visually more complex traditional Chinese script. This study investigated this question in three conditions: a baseline monocolor condition, a word segmentation condition where words were marked by alternating text colors, and a nonword segmentation condition. By tracking the eye movements of 76 older readers, we found a robust interference effect from nonword segmentation across all reading and oculomotor measures. In contrast, benefits of word segmentation cues were strikingly specific, emerging only for readers with lower vocabulary knowledge and for words with clear, unambiguous boundaries. This reveals that the utility of explicit word boundary cues depends on a dynamic interplay between visual processing and vocabulary knowledge. These findings have important implications. Theoretically, they underscore that models of reading should account for word boundary ambiguity and readers’ experience. Practically, the development of assistive reading technologies needs to be tailored to the needs of less proficient readers, who benefit most from external support.

records.title: Reconstructive Threshold Philosophy: Pre-Action Capture, Living Constraint, and Founder Entropy
records.abstract: This essay proposes Reconstructive Threshold Philosophy as a framework for analyzing the interval before action: the moment in which an individual, institution, platform, machine-mediated system, wound, public room, or symbolic frame may begin to move before judgment has returned. Its central claim is that many failures of agency begin prior to visible decision, in pre-action capture: the seizure of attention, interpretation, affect, available motion, institutional possibility, and technical affordance before the subject, office, public, or user experiences itself as choosing. This journal-polish revision preserves the clarification of the living interval. It keeps Manfred Frank as a controlled interlocutor for the distinction between a living capacity and its later objectification, while making explicit that RTF translates that warning structurally rather than ontologically. The essay also distinguishes Frank’s ontological limit from RTF’s structural limit: consciousness is not reducible to an observed object, while the pre-action interval is not protected by being displayed as a marker of judgment, review, delay, room-awareness, or aliveness. RTF instead treats living capacity as situated and temporal: inherited rooms carry momentum, present rooms distribute force, and new frames alter direction before action binds. The vocabulary of the living must therefore remain answerable to dynamic tests of room-motion and threshold pulse rather than degenerating into post-truth markers. This essay does not claim originality in the broad diagnosis that persons, institutions, corrective movements, technologies, liberating forms, or founding names can themselves become captured. Nor does it claim originality in the general demand that knowledge, institutions, and methods remain revisable. Its narrower contribution is the conjunction of three demands. First, the corrective itself must be audited re-entrantly: a brake, helper, method, guardrail, founding name, democratic room, philosophical vocabulary, or machine-facing safeguard must be examined for whether it has become the capture it was meant to prevent. Second, the same failure must be tested across scale: body, habit, family, bureaucracy, public crowd, platform, institution, machine interface, and inherited founding structure. Third, contemporary machine-mediated life makes a temporal failure newly visible: a frame can now be personalized, polished, ranked, retrieved, cited, and sometimes bound to action inside the interval between prompt and answer. The essay clarifies threshold as a family of intervals - pre-action, counter-threshold, machine, room, democratic, and post-threshold - and distinguishes threshold sensitivity from reconstructive discipline: the first names the perceptual capacity to notice the interval before a frame becomes binding; the second names the operative practice of rebuilding the frame once the interval has been seen. Its temporal, counterfactual, and situated axes orient this perception without turning it into a new faculty, checklist, or second originality claim. The essay develops this argument through linked concepts: pre-action capture, the living interval, room-motion, threshold pulse, the living brake, threshold sensitivity, reconstructive discipline, assistance without occupation, machine-facing threshold ethics, room-formation, democratic threshold capacity, distributed threshold capacity, founder entropy, and post-threshold stewardship. It argues that the framework is needed in a world where rooms scale through machines: a frame that once lived inside a family, sect, bureaucracy, party, institution, platform, or movement can now be translated into interfaces, retrieval systems, rankings, recommendations, policy layers, and autonomous tool-use. AI is not treated as a conscious threshold subject, but as both an operational stress test and, where authority has been delegated, a non-conscious operational actor: a system whose classifications, plans, tool calls, and machine-to-machine handoffs may compress or leave intact the interval before judgment, and may bind physical or virtual environments before fresh human review returns. Founder entropy is treated here not as the framework’s apex principle, but as its macro-scale decay test: whether a founding name, corrective form, institution, platform, or protective doctrine has begun to attack the interval it was built to preserve. In v17.3.5 this macro-scale decay is explicitly linked to distributed threshold capacity: the social ability of many persons across many rooms to preserve the interval before action without transferring political judgment to a caste, founder, priesthood, party, technocracy, platform, market, or machine. The expanded argument develops decision sovereignty as a secondary normative synthesis rather than a fourth pillar. It names the preservation of reason-giving, contestability, bounded authority, responsibility, and repair as action moves from frame to authorisation, execution, and effect. Sovereignty here does not mean unlimited human command or a nominal veto. It means that neither a technical system nor an institution may invisibly occupy the capacities to reopen a frame, examine evidence, limit delegated power, interrupt action, or answer for consequences. Its governing test remains accountable motion, not sovereignty elevated into a new source of command. Version v18.3.0 preserves the v18.0.0 clarification architecture, the v17.3.7 political-somatic architecture, and the v18.1.3 Section 14 compression while retaining the Section 5 account of the living interval, marker-capacity substitution, room-motion, threshold pulse, and the anti-aura tests for living vocabulary. It does not add a new pillar, threshold family, hinge, machine doctrine, AI-safety taxonomy, implementation standard, or compliance protocol. It keeps distributed threshold capacity as the social-scale maturation of democratic threshold capacity, while clarifying that the separate DTC article narrows the same phrase to socio-technical decision chains and that fast cognition is not itself capture: capture begins when a fast frame, heuristic, classification, or completion becomes binding in an ecology where judgment can no longer inspect, refuse, revise, or repair it. To show how the framework operates, the essay includes a worked example of an AI-assisted institutional triage room. The worked example strengthens the differentia comparison in Section 3 by placing the framework’s binding-point question beside its nearest sociological, cybernetic, pragmatist, critical-theory, and algorithmic-accountability predecessors. The example illustrates how the conjunction of re-entrant audit, cross-scale analysis, and machine-speed capture focuses attention on the binding point at which a corrective mechanism becomes an instrument of capture - a judgment no single predecessor framework is organized to make in that combined form. The essay also strengthens its own limits. It distinguishes Somatic Echo micro-cases from Codex prose; preserves behavioral tests for living rooms; adds an Arendtian objection that pre-action audit may reduce praxis to poiesis; addresses the Adorno-Williams worry that re-entrant audit can become infinite self-administration; and treats threshold slip as an internal risk of this essay itself rather than merely a later misuse by readers. The final claim is neither stillness nor automatic release. It is accountable motion: action that preserves the interval in which judgment can return. At social scale, that interval lives in votes that cannot be weighed by a self-appointed measure-room, in institutions that can reopen a form, in citizens who can refuse contempt, in founders who can become unnecessary, and in machinemediated rooms where fluency is not mistaken for returned judgment.

records.title: Rendimiento neuropsicológico en el trastorno bipolar en eutimia con y sin intentos de suicidio: estudio comparativo con controles sanos
records.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the neuropsychological performance of euthymic bipolar patients with (CIS) and without suicide attempts (SIS), relative to healthy controls (HC). METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 31 patients (CIS n=15; SIS n=16) and 46 independent HC. The battery comprised RAVLT, Rey Complex Figure, WAIS-III Digit Span, TMT-A/B, WCST, Stroop, and COWAT-FAS. CIS–SIS comparisons were conducted with Student’s t tests; CIS/SIS vs HC with Welch’s t tests; two-tailed p values uncorrected for multiplicity. RESULTS: CIS and SIS showed broadly similar performance in episodic memory, forward working memory, Stroop, and verbal fluency; the only significant between-patient difference was a lower number of WCST categories in CIS. Compared with HC, both groups performed worse on verbal memory (RAVLT) and showed slowing on TMT-B. However, a differential pattern emerged: CIS displayed additional deficits in TMT-A and backward digits, whereas SIS did not differ from HC in these tests. Overall, CIS showed significant impairment relative to HC in three of four measures (RAVLT, TMT-A, and backward digits), while SIS differed in two (RAVLT and TMT-B). CONCLUSIONS: Direct CIS–SIS differences were modest (only WCST categories), but contrasts with controls revealed partially distinct profiles. The findings suggest that deficits in processing speed and working memory may be more pronounced in patients with a history of suicide attempts. These results should be interpreted as exploratory, and replication in larger samples and longitudinal designs is warranted.

records.title: Repetition of the Mere Exposure Effect: Sensory Variance's Limiting Function
records.abstract: One of the most well-known and often quoted discoveries in the field of social psychology is the mere exposure effect. This effect, which was first described by Zajonc in 1968, asserts that a person's like of a stimuli increases with exposure. According to Zajonc, organisms typically gravitate toward familiar things and steer clear of unknown ones, and familiarity is a basic mechanism in deciding preferences. Repetition regularly raises liking scores for a variety of neutral stimuli, including geometric forms, pictures, and meaningless words, according to classic research. Over the years, this discovery has been repeated and validated in a number of domains, including as political opinions, consumer behavior, interpersonal attractiveness, and perceptual fluency. The mere exposure effect may not, however, apply to all situations or stimuli. The emotional valence of the stimulus (positive, neutral, or negative emotional content) can be a significant border condition for this effect, according to recent research. According to certain research, the mere exposure effect is very potent when exposed to neutral or slightly positive stimuli, while it diminishes or vanishes completely when exposed to negative stimuli. For instance, Harmon-Jones and Allen (2001) discovered that liking scores for unpleasant images did not rise with the number of repetitions. Similarly, Monahan, Murphy, and Zajonc (2000) demonstrated that repetition only enhanced liking for neutral or positive stimuli, even when they were offered unintentionally; this effect was not observed for negative stimuli. These results imply that avoidance reactions may be triggered by emotionally unpleasant stimuli, therefore familiarity's "fluency" effect may not be enough to boost liking. This circumstance draws attention to a significant gap in the literature: Even though the mere exposure effect is a fairly potent phenomenon, it is unclear under what circumstances this effect either disappears or becomes weaker. Specifically, whether emotional valence is a limiting variable is unclear. By systematically altering emotional valence and retesting the traditional mere exposure effect, this work seeks to close this gap. This method will make it easier for us to comprehend how repetition-based familiarity affects assessments and identify the kinds of stimuli where this effect shouldn't be anticipated. Participants in the study's replication phase will be shown a series of neutral images; some will be shown just once, while others will be shown several times (e.g., five times). Repeated neutral images are expected to obtain increased like scores based on the classic finding. Images having negative emotional content will be used in the study's boundary condition section. It is anticipated that the mere exposure effect will either not be seen or be significantly weaker in negative valence stimuli based on earlier findings in the literature. There are two main ways that this study will add to the body of literature. First, it will enable the use of digital presentation techniques to retest a well-known social psychology finding in a modern sample. When evaluating the consistency of traditional psychological effects in modern settings and with various participant groups, replication studies are crucial. Second, the inclusion of emotional valence as a moderating variable will contribute to theoretical discussions about the relationships between familiarity and emotion and offer a more thorough knowledge of the conditions under which the mere exposure effect functions. If the results validate the hypotheses, they will demonstrate that familiarity only boosts liking for neutral stimuli, whereas emotional content inhibits the familiarity effect for negative stimuli. This finding will contradict the current literature and may indicate that repetition-based liking increases may be independent of emotional valence if, in contrast to predictions, the mere exposure effect is also seen with negative stimuli. By precisely outlining the study's hypotheses, procedures, variables, and analysis strategy prior to data collection, this preregistration seeks to promote a more transparent and trustworthy research process. This will avoid any bias that can result from formulating hypotheses after the fact or from being flexible in the research process.

records.title: Rethinking Knowledge's Impact on the Illusory Truth Effect.
records.abstract: Repeated exposure to information increases receptivity to it, even when prior knowledge is present, according to the illusory truth effect. Fazio et al. provided empirical support for this phenomenon and proposed a model that posited dominance of fluency cues, relative to knowledge utilization. This model better elucidated participants' behaviors than an alternative model assuming precedence of knowledge processes over fluency-related mechanisms. The present research builds on this by refining models and testing them with new and existing data. While reanalysis of existing data revealed comparable performance of both models, new data from two experiments (N = 324), introducing conditions conducive to discerning between the two models, uncovered compelling evidence in support of the model that assumes knowledge processes' precedence. The discrepancy between Fazio et al. and our findings is discussed, and we encourage future research to explore avenues for resolving the relative roles of knowledge and fluency.

records.title: SILENT CONVERSATIONS BETWEEN MIND AND SPACE : NEUROAESTHETIC READINGS OF ARCHITECTURE AND HUMAN ENGAGEMENT WITH THE AESTHETIC TRIAD
records.venue: International Journal of Progressive Research in Engineering Management and Science
records.abstract: Architecture shapes human perception not only through spatial function but also through subconscious aesthetic engagement.This research investigates how architectural design elements-such as symmetry, rhythm, complexity, and spatial hierarchy-influence perceptual and emotional responses within built environments through the lens of neuroaesthetics.Using Anjan Chatterjee's aesthetic triad framework-sensory-motor fluency, emotion-valuation, and knowledge-meaning-the study analyzes how variations in architectural form affect aesthetic preference and perceptual engagement.A mixed analytical methodology combining computational form analysis and behavioral perception testing was employed to evaluate architectural design variants.The findings indicate that specific compositional configurations can significantly enhance perceptual fluency and emotional valuation, suggesting that aesthetic engagement in architecture can be partially predicted through measurable design parameters.The study proposes a practical framework enabling architects to evaluate aesthetic performance during early design stages and integrate neuroaesthetic principles into architectural practice.

records.title: SLOW: Strategic Logical-Inference Open Workspace for Cognitive Adaptation in AI Tutoring
SOCIAL EQUITY IN FILM CRITICISM
Softening Violence with Verse Data
records.abstract: This is the combined data from our experiment that investigated the influences between aesthetic and moral processing in narrative texts. The data is organized by participant and question. Each question was answered using continuous 7-point Likert scales. We specifically looked at whether processing fluency in aesthetics, as modulated by rhyme and meter, and genre expectation, targeted by presentation as poetry or prose, affect the aesthetic and moral processing of narratives. To do so, we created narratives that had 4 levels of violence depicted in them, ranging from "no violence" to "high violence." For each text, we then created 4 versions: aesthetic poetry, non-aesthetic poetry, aesthetic prose, non-aesthetic prose. For these texts, "aesthetic" means that the texts were written with consistent meter and rhyme, while "non-aesthetic" means that the texts did not include consistent rhyme or meter. In our experiment, participants read one of these stories then used 7-point Likert scales to rate the story on the following dimensions: how upsetting the text is; how bad the actions in the text are; how severely the man in the text should be punished; how immoral the actions are; how melodious the language of the text is; how beautiful the language of the text is. Using a generalized linear model in SPSS, we found that violent content predicted higher ratings for how upsetting, punishable, and immoral the actions in the text are, and lower ratings of how beautiful the text is. We also found that both aesthetic quality (rhyme and meter) and presentation as poetry each separately predicted higher ratings for how beautiful and melodious the text was perceived to be. We also found a slight negative but nonsignificant effect of rhyme and meter on how upsetting violence in the texts was perceived to be. Together, these findings support a processing fluency view of aesthetic pleasure. They also suggest that presentation as poetry makes texts be perceived as more beautiful and melodious. Finally, these findings suggest that violence in texts makes those texts be perceived as both more immoral and less beautiful, even though this violence does not affect the perceived melodiousness of the language itself. Overall, these results lend support to the idea that, in texts, aesthetic quality and moral value each have both an intuitive dimension for how they are experienced as well as a rational dimension for how they are judged and assessed. Moreover, we find that while moral and aesthetic judgment remain distinct, they may blend in their experiential processing.

records.title: Sounds easy, looks nice: Crossmodal transfer of auditory processing fluency to visual object preference
records.abstract: Fluent (i.e., rapid and efficient) processing of perceptual objects is vital for humans to successfully navigate their environments. The experience of fluent processing per se tends to trigger positive affect; however, this affect is often misattributed by perceivers to the objects themselves, meaning that easy-to-perceive objects are judged more positively. These fluency-based preference effects have been robustly demonstrated unimodally, and specifically in situations in which fluency and preference are manipulated and measured for the same objects. However, little is known about how this effect operates crossmodally, when manipulations of fluency in one domain are combined with preference judgements for unmanipulated objects in another domain. In six experiments, we manipulated perceptual fluency in a simple auditory task which participants performed whilst viewing visual objects, which they rated for liking. We found that visual objects presented with easier (more fluent) auditory stimuli received higher liking ratings. This effect persisted when a temporal lag was introduced between the auditory/visual components, but was less reliable for static (as opposed to moving) objects. These results show that fluency-based preference effects can operate crossmodally. They have implications for a range of real-world contexts involving preference and attitude change.

records.title: Speech and Language Markers of Bipolar Disorder: Challenges and Opportunities
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinicians aspire to predict the emergence of Bipolar Disorder (BD) in a timely manner. To accomplish this, markers reflecting mental states that can be gathered non-invasively and at large scale are needed. Here, we systematically evaluate evidence relating speech-based markers to mood states in BD. METHODS: We searched Medline and Google Scholar for all published studies in English up to February 2026 on the use of speech markers in BD. We undertook thematic analysis on abstracts using topic modeling and a qualitative gap analysis to identify potential opportunities for future research. RESULTS: 43 out of 867 studies were included after screening. Topic analysis revealed an emerging focus on mapping mood states to automated speech features. Most studies focused on cross-sectional detection of bipolar mood states, or BD as a diagnosis, rather than the prediction of upcoming mood states. Speech features distinguished BD from schizophrenia, depression, and healthy controls. Manic states were characterized by quantifiable measures of pressured speech, derailment, grammatical errors, and word repetition; depressive states by an increased use of personal pronouns, reduced verbal fluency, and speech quantity. Overall, attempts to replicate observations were limited. CONCLUSION: Acoustic and lexical-semantic markers vary with manic, psychotic, or depressive states. At present, the evidence is insufficient for clinical utility in relapse prediction, response monitoring, or diagnosing mixed episodes or state changes in BD. We recommend that future research leverages the growing capabilities of natural language processing through longitudinal and cross-linguistic studies to strengthen the evidence base and advance the clinical utility of speech markers for BD.

records.title: T. S. Eliot and F. R. Leavis: The Value of University Education and English Studies
records.venue: Journal of the T S Eliot Society of Korea
records.abstract: F. R. Leavis’s critical writings on Eliot reveal various interesting perspectives, ranging from high praise to reserved judgments and even harsh criticism. Conversely, Eliot’s critical interest in Leavis is somewhat lukewarm. In the process of exploring the complex and uneven relationship between Eliot and Leavis, this paper examines the functions and value of university education and English studies. Reacting against the Machine Age, each advocates his own ideas of higher education. Leavis proposes that a “real” university should play a key role as a “creative centre,” with “English” serving as a pivotal discipline and interdisciplinary “liaison centre” to counter the perceived threats of the “technologico-Benthamite age.” Eliot’s ideas of education as a critique of his contemporary circumstances are relatively more conservative and less systematic, maintaining the importance of classic and religious education. To conclude, while Leavis’s project of the creative university opens possibilities and is more relevant to our current situation, Eliot enacts a certain linguistic creativity in his poetry and provides a “heuristic” possibility for university education. In their different ways but through their shared beliefs in the value of creativity and literary language, Eliot and Leavis offer insights into the rapidly changing paradigm of education in the twenty-first century.

records.title: Task Design and Intervention Model for Integrating Computational Thinking into Primary Mathematics
records.abstract: The integration of computational thinking (CT) into mathematics education has attracted increasing attention; however, there is limited methodological clarity about how CT can be systematically embedded in primary mathematics instruction. In particular, empirical research linking CT to multi-step mathematical problem-solving remains scarce. This paper presents the design and implementation of a task-based intervention model developed within the DigiMaths4All project. The model incorporates CT into primary mathematics through a structured framework for task selection and design, combined with implementation in a technology-enhanced learning environment (ViLLE). Mathematical tasks focus on arithmetic fluency and multi-step problem solving, while CT tasks are tailored to operationalize key processes such as decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and debugging. The intervention was carried out through a class-based randomized controlled trial in primary education, comparing traditional instruction with technology-supported approaches, including an integrated mathematics CT model. The study uses a mixed-methods approach, incorporating assessments and learning analytics data to examine implementation processes. The main contribution of this paper is methodological. It offers a replicable framework for (1) designing interventions that incorporate CT into mathematics, (2) selecting and constructing aligned task sets, and (3) implementing these tasks within an analytics-driven digital environment. The findings enhance understanding of how CT can be operationalized to support mathematical problem solving in primary education.

records.title: The Concept of Munkar in al-Dhahabī’s Critique of al-Ḥākim’s Hadith Authentication in al-Mustadrak
records.venue: Jurnal Studi Ilmu-ilmu Al-Qur an dan Hadis
records.abstract: The exclusion of certain hadiths by the compilers of al-Shaykhān (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim), despite their acceptance of the same transmitters in other narrations, indicates the presence of particular flaws within those reports. This selective process has generated substantial discussion in the field of hadith criticism, especially around the notion of “authentication according to their conditions.” Scholarly debates have long centered on how such conditions were defined, interpreted, and applied by later critics. This study explores the methodological divergence between al-Ḥākim al-Nīsābūrī (d. 405/1014) and al-Dhahabī (d. 748/1348) concerning the use of Bukhārī and Muslim’s criteria as benchmarks for authenticity. Specifically, it examines hadiths that al-Ḥākim classified as “authentic according to the conditions of al-Shaykhān or one of them,” but which al-Dhahabī subsequently rejected as munkar. Through an inductive-critical approach, the analysis engages six representative cases drawn from al-Mustadrak and Talkhīṣ al-Mustadrak, allowing for a close reading of how both scholars articulated and operationalized their respective standards. The findings suggest that al-Ḥākim’s approach to authentication was often generous, at times overlooking structural and contextual defects, whereas al-Dhahabī’s assessments reflected a stricter evaluative framework. His judgments of munkar frequently rested on the identification of weak transmitters, disrupted isnād structures, or questionable transmission contexts. Beyond highlighting their methodological contrast, this study raises broader questions about the coherence and applicability of “conditions of the Shaykhān” as a category of hadith validation. Rather than closing the debate, the cases underscore the interpretive tensions within classical hadith criticism and invite further inquiry into how later scholars negotiated between textual authority and critical scrutiny.

records.title: The disputed role of knowledge in truth illusions: A critical test based on comparative judgments
records.abstract: It has been argued that the illusory truth effect - the tendency to judge repeated statements as more likely true - persists even when a statement is known to be false, whereas a competing view maintains that knowledge shields against such truth illusions. In this study, we reexamine two models of truth judgment that formalize these opposing perspectives: the fluency-conditional model (FCM), which assumes that repetition-induced fluency can override knowledge, and the knowledge-conditional model (KCM), which assumes that knowledge always takes precedence over fluency, such that fluency only becomes relevant in the complete absence of knowledge. Utilizing a novel two-alternative forced-choice paradigm, we derive and test critical qualitative predictions of each model. The results disconfirm the FCM while the KCM can be maintained. Quantitative assessments of both models corroborate this conclusion and extend it to some alternative model specifications. We further show that the FCM, as per its qualitative predictions, is incompatible with the assumption that repetition leads to a uniform increase in perceived plausibility. A continuous single-process model operating on this assumption aligns with the KCM's predictions but implies a different psychological mechanism. We conclude by outlining avenues for empirically dissociating these theoretical accounts.

records.title: The genesis of reading fluency in beginning readers
The Impact of Digital Media Technology on Aesthetic Experience in Guangzhou Public Art: Examining the Mediating Role of Processing Fluency
records.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 International Conference on Computer Technology, Digital Media and Communication
records.abstract: This study adopts a computational approach to examine how digital media technology (DMT) features influence the aesthetic experience of public art audiences and to test the mediating role of processing fluency. While prior research has explored the sensory and psychological effects of digital art, few have modeled how media parameters—vividness, visual complexity, and interactivity—affect aesthetic outcomes through cognitive mechanisms. A structural equation modeling (SEM) framework was developed by integrating quantifiable media features with processing fluency theory. Based on 417 valid responses from viewers of digital public art in Guangzhou, parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results show that DMT features significantly predict aesthetic experience (β=0.52, p<.001), with processing fluency partially mediating this effect (indirect β=0.21, ≈40% of total). Vividness and visual complexity enhance perceptual and conceptual fluency, fostering pleasure, immersion, and meaning construction, while excessive interactivity weakens experiential continuity. The framework provides a reproducible model linking technological form and psychological mechanism in digital public art.

records.title: The implications of advances in research on motivation for cognitive models
The Inner Life of AI Criticism: Patterns of Resistance to Technological Innovation and the Need for Academic Metacognition
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This paper does not place the capacities or dangers of generative AI at the center of its inquiry. Rather, it asks what is at work within academia when academia criticizes generative AI. Generative AI has clear limitations. It can fabricate references, produce plausible falsehoods, reproduce dominant assumptions, and confuse fluency with understanding. Verification, methodological control, and responsible use are therefore indispensable. This paper does not dismiss criticism of AI itself. The problem is that such criticism does not always arise solely from the pursuit of truth. Technological innovation almost always generates resistance when it unsettles existing forms of authority, institutions, and interest structures. Yet historically, technological innovation has rarely, if ever, been stopped by resistance itself. The crucial question, therefore, is not whether generative AI can simply be rejected, but what such resistance is trying to protect: the conditions of truth-seeking, or the status, credentials, authority, habitual procedures, and existing boundaries of participation that have governed academic legitimacy. When academia criticizes AI without examining its own inner disposition, that criticism becomes risky. On the surface, it may invoke legitimate concerns: misinformation, plagiarism, declining intellectual discipline, research ethics, and the burden placed on peer review. Yet beneath these concerns, institutional self-defense may also be operating: a desire to control who is permitted to produce knowledge. In such cases, criticism of AI may appear to defend truth-seeking while actually distancing academia from the original vocation of scholarship. Scholarship is not the preservation of authority, but the continual opening of inquiry toward truth. Knowledge is not the property of any institution or professional class; it is a public process formed through evidence, verification, criticism, and revision. When evaluation shifts from evidence and testability toward affiliation, form, and procedural purity, academia risks becoming less a guardian of knowledge than a manager of access to knowledge. The consequence is not merely the exclusion of low-quality intellectual output. Immature but valuable questions, unfamiliar intuitions from outside institutions, and hypotheses not yet legible within existing frameworks may also be prematurely dismissed. Far from protecting scholarly quality, such self-defense narrows the sources of inquiry, weakens the revisability of knowledge, and damages academia’s own credibility and adaptive capacity. Generative AI lowers the costs of reading, translation, literature organization, drafting, and hypothesis formation, thereby widening the entry points into academic knowledge production. This development brings real risks, including the proliferation of low-quality discourse. But it also reveals that knowledge cannot be enclosed within institutional boundaries alone. What is needed, therefore, is neither the uncritical acceptance of AI-generated work nor its exclusion in advance, but a redesign of academic evaluation around the quality of questions, verifiability of evidence, conceptual structure, openness to criticism, and responsibility for judgment. The question posed by AI is not only whether machines can think. It is whether academia, when criticizing AI, can also criticize its own inner motives. In an age of unstoppable technological innovation, what is being tested is not only the intelligence of AI, but the metacognitive capacity of academia itself.

records.title: The interrelationship between the Scientific Field and Internationalization in light of technological fluency
The Purloined Letter of “友”: A Critique of Ezra Pound’s Poetics of Translation
The Reverse Turing Test: A Three-Stage Protocol for Detecting AI-Mediation Signatures in Human Text and Their Propagation to Model Training (v1.1)
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: The Turing Test asked whether a machine could produce text indistinguishable from a human's. This paper asks the reverse: whether humans, after sustained interaction with AI systems, now produce text that bears the detectable statistical signature of having passed through machine cognition — including in writing produced entirely without AI assistance. The model-collapse literature (Shumailov et al. 2024; Briesch et al. 2023; Gerstgrasser et al. 2024) establishes that recursive training on synthetic data produces measurable model degradation. It operates on a clean assumption: synthetic data is the contamination; human data is the refresh. Three recent lines of work suggest the assumption is failing. Padmakumar and He (2024), Doshi and Hauser (2024, Hedges' g = -0.86 for collective novelty), and Anderson et al. (2024) document that AI-mediated human text exhibits population-level diversity reduction even when humans are the final authors. This paper specifies the experimental protocol that would test the joint hypothesis these literatures imply but have not yet closed: that training on AI-mediated human text — including unaided text from cognitively-habituated writers — produces model-collapse signatures comparable to, though plausibly slower than, purely synthetic training data. The central methodological claim is that the effect is not in the means but in the tails. AI mediation does not primarily shift the average lexical, syntactic, or semantic properties of text; it thins the high-perplexity tails. Prior mean-comparison designs have been looking for the effect in the wrong statistical location. The naive design — heavy-AI-user corpus versus non-user corpus — is insufficient. It conflates mediation status with eight confounding variables: demographic selection, cognitive-style selection, domain and genre distribution, era and period, background environmental mediation, acute versus habituated mediation timescales, within-person versus across-person variance, and compensatory overcorrection. The paper specifies a three-stage protocol designed to isolate the mediation effect from each. Stage 1 — The Reverse Turing Test: Validation of a Mediation Index that detects mediation signatures in arbitrary text using tail-focused distributional statistics (kurtosis comparison, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, quantile regression), validated against observationally-grounded ground truth and scored against a frozen pre-2020 language model as a naive statistical witness. Stage 2 — Habituation: Three coordinated sub-studies measuring whether mediation signatures appear in verified-unaided writing (2A: cross-sectional with Mediation Depth Index across five subscales), whether AI-mediated retrieval shapes subsequent unaided writing even without production assistance (2B: retrieval-isolation), and whether the signature propagates beyond writing into oral storytelling (2C: cross-modal transfer). Stage 3 — Training Cascade: Model training on corpora stratified by Mediation Index score across four conditions (H0 unmediated, H1 acute-mediated, H2 residual-mediated unaided from habituated writers, S synthetic), with collapse-axis evaluation focused on tail-recovery rather than mean-fluency. H2 is the critical condition: text that is operationally human (no AI in the room during production) but bears the statistical signature of habituated cognitive production. The paper does not run the experiment. It specifies it with the discipline required for the result to be informative under any of six distinguishable outcome patterns. The Mediation Index, the Mediation Depth Index, and the corpus-stratification schema are designed to be released as open instruments so that independent groups can replicate, refute, or extend the work. If the strong hypothesis is confirmed, the operational implications include: pre-2022 text becomes a strategic resource with calculable economic value; training-data curation gains a continuous mediation-status axis beyond the synthetic/human binary; the half-life of the human-data refresh becomes calculable; mediation metadata becomes a corpus-tagging standard; and low-mediation reserves require substantial preservation effort. The work sits in the third register of the Meaning Feudalism series (Sharks 2026, DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.19487009 and 10.5281/zenodo.20581444). The first paper diagnosed the platform-as-jurisdiction move at the agent-security register. The second diagnosed it at the optimization-jurisdiction register. The Reverse Turing Test, if confirmed, identifies the third register: the cognitive pre-shaping of the population that produces the training inputs to the composition layer — the enclosure of cognition itself. records.title: The sweet spot of seeing: A categorization-based account of visual aesthetic pleasure.
records.abstract: Aesthetic pleasure is shaped by many visual attributes, including prototypicality, fluency, complexity, symmetry, and self-relevance, but it is unclear why such diverse factors all influence liking. I propose that a major component of visual aesthetic pleasure is an epiphenomenon of categorization in the visual system, constrained by the metabolic cost of neural activity. In this view, successfully recognizing a stimulus as a member of a category is intrinsically rewarding because it supports perception, generalization, and planning, and aesthetic pleasure partly reflects the summed effect of many local rewards for successful categorization across the visual hierarchy. At the same time, neural activity costs energy, so that strongly driven, cluttered, or statistically extreme displays incur costs that can make them aversive even when they are easily interpretable. The "sweet spot of seeing" (3S) model formalizes visual pleasure as a compromise between categorization-based reward and metabolic expense. It offers a unifying explanation for prototype effects, fluency and mere exposure, mid-level regularities such as symmetry and good continuation, and visual discomfort. The model links classic inverted-U relations between complexity and liking to a concrete trade-off between information and cost, and it makes specific predictions for how aesthetic preferences change due to expertise or fatigue. While integrating recent evidence that lower-cost representations in categorization-trained neural networks and human visual cortex predict higher aesthetic ratings, the 3S model leaves room for later, reflective, self-relevant, and culturally informed forms of aesthetic experience that recruit broader neural systems.

records.title: Time in Text: Differentiating Instruction for Intermediate Students Struggling with Word Recognition
records.abstract: When students read below grade level, teachers are caught between two goals: (a) keeping text complexity high for comprehension instruction and (b) ensuring students are spending time in text, recognizing words themselves. This article informs the problem with research-based recommendations. Recently I was in a K–5 elementary school, one in which many intermediate-grade students had not passed their state outcome measure for reading. Following a state plan, the teachers were doing high-intensity tutoring in small groups with these intermediate-grade students struggling with reading. One fourth-grade teacher shared a concern that went something like this: “This tutoring requires us to do the interventions using ‘on grade-level content’ but I have fourth graders who are reading on a first-grade reading level. Are they supposed to read grade level texts or am I supposed to just read it to them? That's fine if I am supposed to read it to them but at what point do they practice reading?” Boy, I felt her pain. On the one hand, I had seen the devastating effects of limiting third–fifth-grade students with below-grade level word recognition skills, to simple, decodable books of 100–200 words. It meant they did not get the rich vocabulary, content knowledge, and advanced comprehension from grade-level materials. On the other hand, I worried about “exposure to grade-level” materials replacing time in text, the kind that builds accurate, fluent decoding and eventual automaticity. In fact, based on my observations, in many classrooms, exposure to grade-level text for comprehension was coming at the cost of systematic, explicit, decoding and morphology instruction. There are beginning readers in grades 3–5, readers who do not have mastery of the most common graphemes and morphemes that children typically solidify in K–1. There are also readers who have partial knowledge with decoding gaps that impede their ability to recognize words in text. I started to imagine an impending tsunami of sorts when students arrived in middle schools thinking like champs but unable to recognize words. Although reading aloud across K–12 is a critical practice, it should not supplant student reading. Read-alouds in the secondary school should not be the primary access to text for students. Many teachers are caught between keeping the challenge and complexity of text content high for comprehension and ensuring that students are spending time in text, recognizing words themselves so that they will become fluent, accurate, and expressive readers. In this article, I address four issues that classroom teachers face in dealing with below-grade decoders: (1) When to mediate student word recognition in grade-level texts; (2) How to mediate word recognition in grade-level text; (3) How to differentiate texts, when necessary, to ensure time-in-text; and (4) How to close decoding gaps. This article focuses on students in a given grade who find it challenging to recognize words in grade-level texts and it uses several terms, reading, grade-level text, text access, and word recognition scaffolding. Because these terms can have different meanings, I provide research-based definitions to each in the Table 1. Reading = Word Recognition × Comprehension Reading involves two fundamental processes: word recognition and comprehension, a model called the Simple View (Gough & Tunmer, 1986). From this theoretical model, reading happens only when students are engaged in both word recognition and comprehension. Word recognition refers to the process of identifying a word's oral pronunciation using a variety of mechanisms (e.g., decoding, structural analysis, and automatic recognition). According to Gough and Tunmer (1986), word recognition is fast, automatic, and importantly, in their model, it precedes language comprehension. Decoding is using the relationships between phonemes and graphemes, the alphabetic system, to translate words into their oral pronunciations. Decoding is sounding out words, a behavior that orthographically maps words and enables cognitive storage and retrieval. The Active View of reading further unpacks word recognition and language comprehension; identifying bridging processes such as fluency, morphology, and cognitive flexibility that reflect an overlap of word recognition and comprehension (Duke & Cartwright, 2021) In this article, text exposure refers to a strategy to give readers access to the words in text because they cannot recognize a large proportion of words. In short, it is someone else recognizing the words. Shared reading activities such as teacher read-alouds and computer-generated output can compensate for deficits or nascent skills in decoding. This access provides a temporary entrée to the meaning, vocabulary, and ideas in a text so that students can participate in vocabulary, content, and comprehension instruction. Exposure to grade-level texts and their content is a critical component of instruction to maintain high-level comprehension and vocabulary when students are unable to recognition a minimum threshold of words in a text (Montag & MacDonald, 2015). One of the pivotal questions that teachers must answer with students is when to scaffold word recognition in challenging texts and when the word recognition demands are too high for any benefit to be derived from scaffolding. In this section, I provide guidance in the following areas: (a) studies that used word accuracy to mediate word recognition, (b) studies that used reading level, and (c) caveats about mediating word recognition supports. Although flawed and perhaps overvalued, the approaches to reader-text matching provide a place to start (Mesmer, 2008; Reutzel & Fawson, 2022). The two approaches are (a) word accuracy levels and (b) reading level matches. In the word accuracy approach, also called “individual reader-text match,” the percentage of words read accurately is used to determine a match (Amendum et al., 2018) (Note. All attempts to connect readers with texts will be estimates. As a student reads and a teacher responds, reader-text matches are adjusted). The word accuracy levels that are widely used today emanated from Betts' 1946 study, which suggested 95–99% for instructional (INS) level text, 99–100% for independent (IND) level, and 90% for frustrational (FRUS). These accuracy levels have shifted a bit to 90–95% for INS and 96–100% for IND. Educators have rightly questioned these levels due to the lack of strong research to support them and several studies suggest that, under the right conditions they can be flexed (See Halladay, 2012; Strong et al., 2018). A 2010 study tested the influence of initial accuracy levels on the word recognition, decoding, vocabulary, and comprehension of second to fourth graders struggling with reading (O'Connor et al., 2010). Students were randomly assigned to one of four groups in which they practiced reading texts that were (a) at an IND level initially (92–100%), (b) difficult level initially (80–90% accuracy), or (c) an untreated control. For a period of 20 weeks, students in the independent and difficult groups practiced reading to an adult listener who provided difficult words for them when the students stumbled. Both groups reading text had better reading rates, word recognition, and comprehension skills than the untreated control group. Interestingly, there were no significant differences in growth between the different text levels. Both groups of students, even those reading texts at 80% initially, benefited. However, second-grade and fourth-grade texts were different. Researchers found that second-grade texts had more overlapping or repeated words across passages meaning that second graders were rereading more previously seen words. The study suggested that, with an adult nearby, students can handle texts that they originally read with as low as 80% word accuracy but in second grade, the texts should have some word-level controls and repetition across passages. A 2007 study examined comprehension and word accuracy of 64 “language minority1” or multilingual (ML) first graders, participating in one-on-one tutoring (Ehri et al., 2007). Researchers analyzed progress based on if the students initially read the books at IND (98–100%), INS (90–97%), or FRUS (<90%) accuracy levels, and found that multilingual learners appeared to make the greatest gains in word reading and comprehension in IND-level texts, ones that they initially read at 98–100% accuracy. This suggested that higher levels of accurate word recognition were necessary for comprehension with students learning English. This makes sense, the demands of both recognizing words and then connecting those L2 words to meanings may tax reading comprehension of MLs. With the second approach, the reading level match, also called “group or grade/text match,” a student's reading level is obtained in grades or Lexiles and matched to a text in the same units. With mixed results, researchers have tested the impact of having students read one, two, three, or even four levels above their levels (Brown et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2000; O'Connor et al., 2002; Stahl & Heubach, 2005). Two studies investigated the impact of a partner reading invention on second graders (Brown et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2000). In both these studies, students were paired with more capable peers and asked to read 15 minutes per day for 95 days. The students read together sitting side by side with one smooth finger tracking the print. They were told to keep their eyes on the words, read together, and identify difficult words for help later. In the first study, second graders who read at a pre-primer level initially were assigned texts at the following levels (a) on-level (PrePrimer); (b) two grades above level (first); and (c) four grades above level (second). The most improvement was for students reading two grades above—second graders reading first-grade materials (Morgan et al., 2000). A modified replication was conducted in 2017 with second graders reading texts at two, three, or four “levels” about their measured reading level. There were no effects for the more capable peers, but the readers being assisted, those working at two “levels” above their instructional levels, had the best gains in fluency and comprehension (Brown et al., 2018). Another study manipulated text with third through fifth graders struggling with reading. Within a tutoring program students were randomly assigned to read texts either (a) at their assigned to reading level; or (b) at their grade levels (~2 levels above). Fluency was best with texts matched to actual reading levels not grade-level texts (O'Connor et al., 2002). The fourth study, a robust, 2-year project, found positive effects of increasing text difficulty on the comprehension of second graders (Stahl & Heubach, 2005). The Fluency Oriented Reading Instruction (FORi) had students rereading the same text four to seven times over a week. Teachers presented texts using many different techniques and provided a series of supports (see below) and the intervention improved comprehension and reading levels. A final study with fourth graders functioning below level used sets of texts with different levels to build comprehension and vocabulary around social studies concepts (Gelzheiser, 2005). Students chose books and read them with volunteers over 50 sessions. Book choices were adjusted for ability and interest. The exploratory study found that readers' entering decoding skills, experience of the volunteer, and text difficulty levels were predictive of gains in reading achievement. One final consideration in using the reading level approach is to think about the standard error of measure with readability formulas. A standard error of measurement (SEM) is the range around which the true difficulty of a text is. Most formulas have a SEM of 0.5–1 grades (Mesmer, 2008). This means that if a text is estimated to be at a 3.3 grade level, its true difficulty may be as high as 4.3 or as low as 2.3. What this suggests is that if a text is within one grade level of a student's reading level, mediating word recognition might be productive, particularly if the student is typically developing. The literature provides additional insights about mediating word recognition in grade-level text. Many studies, for example, confirm that increases above one grade level, without support are not beneficial (Amendum et al., 2016; Mesmer & Hiebert, 2015). A literature review examined the relationship between text difficulty, comprehension, and fluency (Amendum et al., 2018). Overall, the findings showed negative or nonsignificant relationships between increases in text difficulty and comprehension and fluency. Two additional studies tested the impact of students reading above level without support (Amendum et al., 2016; Mesmer & Hiebert, 2015). Researchers examined the comprehension of over 600 students in grades 1–3 independently reading materials at and well above grade level (Amendum et al., 2016). Students reading materials well above grade level, even if reading with high levels of accuracy, had significantly lower levels of comprehension. In another study, researchers tested the comprehension of third graders at the end of the school year. Students independently read texts at two lengths (200 vs.1000 words) and three levels: second (400 L), third–fourth (600 L), and fifth (800 L) (Mesmer & Hiebert, 2015). When third graders read fifth grade-level materials, they achieved 50–57% comprehension. When they read third-to fourth-grade materials, they comprehended 64–66% and 71–84% in second-grade materials. Make sure that children have solid foundational skills in decoding—say through a high first-grade or a beginning second-grade level— before increasing the complexity of the texts used to teach reading… The caution given here for young readers also would make sense for older readers who still decode like kindergartners or first graders. Don't worry about taking students beyond “instructional level” texts until they are able to decode as well as a successful first-grader (p. 22). This perspective was also reflected in a piece by Reutzel and Fawson (2022) who pointed out the developmental importance of decoding accuracy and self-confidence. They wrote, “In the earliest stages of reading acquisition, teachers do well to select texts that act as scaffolds for developing young students' reading foundation skills as well as to bolster their collective sense of self-efficacy as early readers. (p. 498).” An experimental study with second and third graders struggling with reading, supported this perspective. Researchers analyzed all the words read by students and found that texts with more complex vowel and morphemic patterns were associated with compromised letter sound, fluency, and comprehension performance (Vadasy & Sanders, 2009). Incomplete decoding knowledge affects fluency and comprehension. Essentially text levels are less flexible with beginning readers who do not have a command of the most common graphemes. Educators can use a variety of research-based techniques to help below-grade decoders to engage in both parts of the reading equation themselves. I will highlight three of them here. Fluency Oriented Reading Instruction (Stahl & Heubach, 2005) and Wide-Reading FORi (Kuhn et al., 2006) are research-tested instructional routines that scaffold not only word recognition but also fluency and comprehension in grade-level texts. In their 2-year study, Stahl and Heubach (2005) reorganized a basal reading program, to include whole-group repeated readings, partner reading, and silent reading opportunities with self-selected texts. FORi resulted in significant gains in reading levels for all but two second-grade students who began the year at the primer level or higher, and half of those students who started below the primer level. These students were reading on grade level by the end of the year. Students made 1.88 year's growth in Year 1 and 1.77 year's growth in Year 2. The program's largest gains were on measures of rate and accuracy, factors that free up working memory so readers can focus on comprehension. Wide-Reading FORi, a modified replication of FORi, substituted wide reading, increased reading volume, for repeated reading. In Table 2, shown below, FORi components are summarized (Stahl & Heubach, 2005). Read along Story discussion Echo read Partner reading Read at home Whole-class choral read Partner reading A second technique for scaffolding word recognition, as well as comprehension is the text set (Gelzheiser, 2005; Lupo et al., 2020). Researchers applied this technique within content areas such as social studies or science to build knowledge. Difficult texts with rich, advanced vocabulary build knowledge and are paired with more accessible texts that build reader capacity and efficacy—the sense that I can read this and learned something. In one study, the set was built with following four types: (a) controlled vocabulary texts (INS or IND); (b) picture books (FRUS); (c) chapter books (FRUS); and (d) informational texts (FRUS) (Gelzheiser, 2005). Another study used the following types: (a) target text, a dense, challenging textbook chapter; (b) a visual text to convey information graphically; (c) a hook text, to show relevance and create excitement; and d) an informational text with word-level controls (e.g., Newsela). In both studies, students read all types of texts within the set. Often, the more challenging texts were after the easier texts and were sometimes read aloud. The approach worked because a diversity of materials with the same content presented vocabulary and information repeatedly and at different levels of depth. Students may read easier materials that have less depth of concept, but those materials produce background to access more challenging texts. A third approach to scaffolding may seem rather odd, even counter-productive, but under certain circumstances, it appears to have some benefits (O'Connor et al., 2010). The approach involves simply pronouncing a challenging word for a student.
